In situations such as examples, prototype code, and tests, it’s more appropriate to write code that panics instead of returning a

It’s advisable to have your code panic when it’s possible that your code could end up in a bad state. In this context, a

text.v: If someone calls your code and passes in values that don’t make sense, it’s best to return an error if you can so that the user of the library can decide what they want to do in that case. However, in cases where continuing could be insecure or harmful, the best choice might be to call
and alert the person using your library to the bug in their code so that they can fix it during development. Similarly,
is often appropriate if you’re calling external code that is out of your control and returns an invalid state that you have no way of fixing.
However, when failure is expected, it’s more appropriate to return a
call. Examples include a parser being given malformed data or an HTTP request returning a status that indicates you have hit a rate limit. In these cases, returning a
indicates that failure is an expected possibility that the calling code must decide how to handle.

When your code performs an operation that could put a user at risk if it’s called using invalid values, your code should verify the values are valid first and panic if the values aren’t valid. This is mostly for safety reasons: Attempting to operate on invalid data can expose your code to vulnerabilities. This is the main reason the standard library will call
if you attempt an out-of-bounds memory access: Trying to access memory that doesn’t belong to the current data structure is a common security problem. Functions often have

: Their behavior is only guaranteed if the inputs meet particular requirements. Panicking when the contract is violated makes sense because a contract violation always indicates a caller-side bug, and it’s not a kind of error you want the calling code to have to explicitly handle. In fact, there’s no reasonable way for calling code to recover; the calling
need to fix the code. Contracts for a function, especially when a violation will cause a panic, should be explained in the API documentation for the function.

However, having lots of error checks in all of your functions would be verbose and annoying. Fortunately, you can use Rust’s type system (and thus the type checking done by the compiler) to do many of the checks for you. If your function has a particular type as a parameter, you can proceed with your code’s logic knowing that the compiler has already ensured that you have a valid value. variants: It will only have one case for definitely having a value. Code trying to pass nothing to your function won’t even compile, so your function doesn’t have to check for that case at runtime. Another example is using an unsigned integer type such as

Let’s take the idea of using Rust’s type system to ensure that we have a valid value one step further and look at creating a custom type for validation. Recall the guessing game in Chapter 2 in which our code asked the user to guess a number between 1 and 100. We never validated that the user’s guess was between those numbers before checking it against our secret number; we only validated that the guess was positive. In this case, the consequences were not very dire: Our output of “Too high” or “Too low” would still be correct. But it would be a useful enhancement to guide the user toward valid guesses and have different behavior when the user guesses a number that’s out of range versus when the user types, for example, letters instead.

Rust’s error-handling features are designed to help you write more robust code. The
macro signals that your program is in a state it can’t handle and lets you tell the process to stop instead of trying to proceed with invalid or incorrect values. The
enum uses Rust’s type system to indicate that operations might fail in a way that your code could recover from. You can use
to tell code that calls your code that it needs to handle potential success or failure as well. Using
in the appropriate situations will make your code more reliable in the face of inevitable problems.
